questions.stem: What makes a good product description for a business plan?

options.text: Describing specifically what the product or service is and what it includes
Naming as many products as possible

questions.explanation: A good product description is specific: it explains what the product or service is, what it includes, and what makes it distinct. Vague descriptions like 'good stuff' tell the reader nothing useful.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 60–65 on products and services

questions.stem: Listing product features is enough to show you understand your customer's needs.
questions.explanation: Product features describe what the product does. Customer needs describe the problem or want from the customer's perspective. You need to explain WHY the customer needs this — not just what it does.

options.text: What makes your product different from or better than alternatives
Selling the same product as everyone else
Having the most products in your shop

questions.explanation: Product differentiation is what sets your product apart from competitors or alternatives. It could be quality, uniqueness, price, service, convenience, or any feature that gives customers a reason to choose you.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 65–70 on competition and differentiation

questions.stem: Match each statement to the correct product concept.

pairs.left: No other local bakery uses traditional methods

questions.explanation: A complete product overview covers three things: what you sell (description), why customers want it (need), and why they would choose you over alternatives (differentiation).

questions.stem: If no one else sells exactly the same product, you have no competition.
questions.explanation: Competition includes any alternative way customers could meet the same need. Even if no one sells exactly what you do, customers can choose substitutes, do without, or solve their problem differently.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 65–70 on competition and differentiation

questions.stem: Why must your product description be consistent with your earlier gates?

options.text: It doesn't need to be — each gate is separate
Because the product must match the business idea, ownership structure and location you already chose
Because you cannot change your mind about anything

questions.explanation: Your business plan must be internally consistent. The product you describe in this gate must logically fit with the business idea (Gate 0), ownership structure (Gate 1), and location (Gate 2) you already chose.

questions.stem: Which statement best shows a customer need?

options.text: Our cake has three layers and costs $45
Parents need impressive birthday cakes but don't have time to bake
The cake comes in a nice box

questions.explanation: Option B describes the customer's problem from their perspective: they need something (impressive cake) but face a barrier (no time to bake). The other options describe product features, not customer needs.

questions.stem: 'Food products' is a specific enough product description for a business plan.
questions.explanation: 'Food products' is a category, not a specific product. A business plan needs to say exactly what food — for example, 'handmade gourmet chocolates in gift boxes' is specific enough.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 60–65 on products and services
